query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing up to 1 atomic percent of boron into a eutectic AlCoCrFeNi- based high-entropy alloy refines its interfacial microstructure, thereby increasing both yield strength (by about 20%) and tensile ductility (by about 10%) relative to an undoped baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic high-entropy alloy with no boron addition.
generation.intervention: Melt-process the alloy under inert atmosphere with 0–1 at.% boron added, followed by homogenization at approximately 1100 °C and optional moderate forging before final cooling.
generation.conditions: Materials prepared by arc or induction melting under inert conditions; homogenized at ~1100 °C; room-temperature mechanical testing to assess yield strength and ductility.
generation.structural_mediator: Stabilization and refinement of boride-containing interfaces that reduce grain-boundary energy and enhance dislocation accommodation.
generation.mechanism: Minor boron additions promote finely distributed borides at boundaries, leading to both a refined microstructure and reduced crack nucleation sites, thereby raising strength and delaying the onset of brittleness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Simultaneous improvement of yield strength by ~20% and elongation by ~10% compared to an undoped reference.
generation.baseline: Undoped AlCoCrFeNi eutectic high-entropy alloy subjected to the same melt processing, homogenization, and testing conditions.
generation.boundary: Beneficial effects are expected for boron additions below ~1 at.%. Excessive additions may induce coarse boride precipitates that reduce ductility or cause processing difficulties.
generation.uncertainty: Exact magnitudes of strength and ductility improvements remain to be confirmed experimentally; the efficacy may vary with compositional details and heat treatment protocols.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce a series of AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic high-entropy alloys with boron content varied incrementally from 0 to 1 at.%. Perform identical homogenization and forging treatments followed by standard tensile tests.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ductility (elongation to fracture) at room temperature
Microstructure characterization (e.g., X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy) to verify boride phases and assess interfacial morphologies
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, across the series, the addition of boron does not produce any simultaneous increase in both yield strength and ductility compared to the undoped control, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. chosen.technique: Arc or induction melting with careful B additions, followed by standard forging/heat treatment
chosen.conditions: Eutectic AlCoCrFeNi-based alloy, <1 at.% B doping, homogenization at ~1100 °C, air cooling or moderate forging
chosen.why: Testable hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of boron (<1 at.%) into a eutectic AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy refines its interfacial microstructure, enhancing both strength and ductility. The proposed mechanism is that B additions promote stable borides and reduce grain-boundary energy, hindering dislocation motion and crack nucleation. We expect a ~20% increase in yield strength and ~10% improvement in ductility compared to an undoped baseline when tested under standard homogenization and forging conditions. Prior studies on multi-principal element alloys and advanced steels show that minor B doping can refine microstructures and improve fracture resistance. This hypothesis can be falsified by systematically varying B content from 0 to 1 at.% and performing tensile and impact tests alongside microstructural characterization: if no improvements in both strength and ductility are observed, the hypothesis would be disproven.
